F1.quote: The IPTC has launched Metawatch , a free, open monitor that checks every month whether more than 500 news publishers in 122 countries keep the credits, captions and rights information embedded in their photographs.
F1.claim: the monitor defined by its operator: free, open, monthly, more than 500 publishers in 122 countries, whether they keep the credits, captions and rights information embedded in their photographs
F1.lineage: what it is: a free, open monthly monitor of whether news publishers keep embedded photo metadata

F2.quote: The first results show how little has changed since 2018, which publishers have fixed their sites, and why keeping metadata matters more than ever now that AI companies are crawling the web.
F2.claim: the operator's summary of its first results: little changed since 2018; some publishers fixed; metadata matters more now that AI companies crawl the web
F2.lineage: findings: credit and the scored fields (October 2026)

F3.locus: 'Credits are lost between camera and reader' (heading and ¶2)
F3.quote: Credits are lost between camera and reader … In practice, most of it is gone by the time a reader sees the picture. Content management systems re-encode images, content delivery networks resize them, and optimisation tools discard anything that looks like unnecessary bytes.
F3.claim: the transformation: credits lost between camera and reader as CMSs re-encode, CDNs resize and optimisation tools discard metadata
F3.lineage: the transformation tested: credit lost between camera and reader

F4.locus: 'Credits are lost between camera and reader' ¶3
F4.quote: When an image is copied, shared or collected by an AI crawler, the embedded metadata is often the only record of where it came from and on what terms it may be used.
F4.claim: why it matters: for a copied, shared or AI-crawled image the embedded metadata is often the only record of origin and terms
F4.lineage: the transformation tested: credit lost between camera and reader

F5.quote: Metawatch checks every month: does the photo metadata survive publication? On the first of each month our well-behaved crawler visits 508 news publishers in 122 countries, takes up to 20 recent articles from each, and reads the lead photograph of every article.
F5.claim: the method: monthly, whether photo metadata survives publication; 508 publishers in 122 countries, up to 20 recent articles each, the lead photograph of each
F5.lineage: the method: the lead photograph of up to 20 articles from each of 508 publishers, scored on the 4 Cs

F6.quote: It checks each image for Exif, IPTC Photo Metadata (in both IIM and XMP form) and C2PA Content Credentials, and scores how each site carry the fields that matter most: creator, caption, copyright and credit line (the “4 Cs”).
F6.claim: what is checked and scored: Exif, IPTC Photo Metadata (IIM and XMP) and C2PA Content Credentials; the score on creator, caption, copyright and credit line, the 4 Cs
F6.lineage: the method: the lead photograph of up to 20 articles from each of 508 publishers, scored on the 4 Cs

F7.quote: The crawler is deliberately light: about 40 to 60 requests per publisher per month, honouring robots.txt and keeping no article text or image files. How it works is documented in full, and every run is published as open data under CC BY 4.0, so anyone can check our numbers or ask their own questions.
F7.claim: a light crawler (40–60 requests per publisher a month, robots.txt honoured, no text or images kept); method documented; every run open data under CC BY 4.0
F7.lineage: open data, cadence and the operator

F8.quote: Metawatch builds on IMATAG’s 2018 State of Image Metadata study and IPTC’s own prototype crawler from 2019 , presented at the 2019 Photo Metadata Conference . This service is different in that we now measure every month, so we can compare trends over time.
F8.claim: its predecessors: IMATAG's 2018 study and the IPTC's 2019 prototype crawler; it differs in measuring every month
F8.lineage: predecessors: IMATAG 2018 and the IPTC prototype crawler of 2019

F9.quote: In 2018 IMATAG found that 8% of editorial images carried a credit or copyright notice. Applying the same test to our October run gives 7.2%. Whatever else has changed in news publishing since then, keeping the photographer’s credit attached to the photograph has not improved.
F9.claim: the headline finding: 7.2% of editorial images with a credit or copyright notice in October 2026 against IMATAG's 8% in 2018; no improvement
F9.lineage: findings: credit and the scored fields (October 2026)

F10.quote: In the October run, 321 of the 425 publishers we could crawl, three out of four kept none of the IPTC fields we score on any image we sampled. Only 11% of the 6,580 images carried any IPTC metadata at all . The field that survives most often is the photographer’s name, on just 7.9% of images; the credit line is on 5.7% and copyright on 5.6%.
F10.claim: 321 of 425 crawlable publishers kept none of the scored fields; 11% of 6,580 images carry any IPTC metadata; creator 7.9%, credit line 5.7%, copyright 5.6%
F10.lineage: findings: credit and the scored fields (October 2026)

F11.quote: It isn’t the CDN’s fault. Images served through Cloudflare, Akamai, CloudFront and Fastly lost their metadata 87% to 95% of the time, but images served with no CDN at all also lost metadata 87% of the time. Stripping appears to happen in the publishing pipeline, which means that publishers can fix it.
F11.claim: the loss through four CDNs (87–95%) matches the loss with no CDN (87%); stripping appears to happen in the publishing pipeline, which publishers can fix
F11.lineage: where the stripping happens: the publishing pipeline

F12.quote: USA Today carried no credit metadata when IMATAG measured it in 2019; in September 95% of its lead photographs carried credit, creator and copyright. Les Echos went from 6% to 75%. … Across the 294 publishers we have measured every month since June, the number keeping any metadata rose from 60 to 67. It is early, but the needle can move.
F12.claim: movement: USA Today from none (2019) to 95% (September 2026); Les Echos 6% to 75%; of 294 publishers measured monthly since June, those keeping any metadata rose from 60 to 67

F13.quote: France tops our October ranking, with an average publisher score of 19.8 out of 100, just ahead of Germany at 19.2. Taiwan enters at third. We rank only countries where we scored more than three publishers, so that one well-run newsroom cannot carry a whole country; 34 countries qualified this month.
F13.claim: the October country ranking (France 19.8, Germany 19.2, Taiwan third) and its rule (more than three publishers scored; 34 countries)

F14.quote: The United States led in September and slipped to fourth in October, but only because two of its best-scoring publishers were out of reach: AP and USA Today began blocking automated access this month. It is a reminder that bot-blocking aimed at AI also shuts out research.
F14.claim: the stated access limit: AP and USA Today blocked automated access in October, moving the United States from first to fourth; bot-blocking aimed at AI also shuts out research
F14.lineage: stated limits: access blocked, the crawler's blind spots

F15.locus: 'AI: a locked front door, an open back door' ¶1–2
F15.quote: Of the 505 publishers whose policies we checked, 234 (46%) block at least one AI crawler in their robots.txt. … But robots.txt protects a website, not a photograph. … IPTC Photo Metadata has a field for exactly this: PLUS Data Mining . Only 15 publishers (3.0%) put it on any image we sampled, and it appears on 0.6% of images overall.
F15.claim: 234 of 505 publishers (46%) block an AI crawler in robots.txt, which protects a site and not a photograph; the PLUS Data Mining field is used by 15 publishers and appears on 0.6% of images
F15.lineage: AI: crawler blocking, the data-mining field, Content Credentials, the AI fields

F16.locus: 'AI: a locked front door, an open back door' ¶3 s1–2
F16.quote: Leaving out IPTC’s own site, 27 of the 6,580 images we analysed carried a C2PA manifest, and all but one were signed by an AI or design tool: OpenAI, Adobe, Canva or Google (the last had a signer we couldn’t read). None came from a camera or a newsroom’s own signing.
F16.claim: 27 of 6,580 images carry a C2PA manifest, all but one signed by an AI or design tool; none from a camera or a newsroom's own signing
F16.lineage: AI: crawler blocking, the data-mining field, Content Credentials, the AI fields

F17.locus: 'AI: a locked front door, an open back door' ¶3 s3–4
F17.quote: Seven images carried an IPTC Digital Source Type saying they had been edited with generative AI, which is exactly the kind of disclosure the field was designed for. Provenance in news photography is arriving first through the tools that make synthetic images, not through the photojournalism that most needs it.
F17.claim: seven images disclose generative-AI editing by Digital Source Type; provenance in news photography arrives first through the tools that make synthetic images
F17.lineage: AI: crawler blocking, the data-mining field, Content Credentials, the AI fields

F18.quote: The fix is usually a setting, not a project. Most image pipelines strip metadata by default to save a few kilobytes; most can be told to keep it.
F18.claim: the fix: a setting; most image pipelines strip metadata by default and can be told to keep it
F18.lineage: where the stripping happens: the publishing pipeline

F19.quote: Metawatch automatically publishes new results on the first of every month.
F19.claim: new results published automatically on the first of every month
F19.lineage: open data, cadence and the operator

F20.quote: Oct 5 2026 … Announcing Metawatch: a monthly check on which news publishers keep photo metadata
F20.lineage: dates: runs from June, a September showing, the October announcement

F21.quote: Metawatch tracks how often major news publishers preserve embedded photo metadata (Exif, IPTC Photo Metadata (in both original IIM format and newer XMP format), and C2PA) on the images they publish. We crawl a curated list of publishers monthly and score the photographs they serve.
F21.claim: the monitor's own page: how often major news publishers preserve embedded photo metadata (Exif, IPTC IIM and XMP, C2PA); a curated list crawled monthly, the served photographs scored
F21.lineage: what it is: a free, open monthly monitor of whether news publishers keep embedded photo metadata

F22.quote: Latest run 2026-10-01 Sites crawled 425 Countries 122 Images analysed 6,580 … Mean IPTC score 5.96 … % with any IPTC 11% % with C2PA 0.5%
F22.claim: the latest run, 2026-10-01: 425 sites, 122 countries, 6,580 images; mean IPTC score 5.96; 11% with any IPTC, 0.5% with C2PA
F22.lineage: findings: credit and the scored fields (October 2026)

F23.quote: How this run’s top 10 ranked in earlier runs … 2026-06-03 2026-07-01 2026-08-01 2026-09-01 2026-10-01 … France: #1 of 26 on 2026-06-03 — score 22.8, 10 publishers
F23.claim: five runs on the overview, the first dated 2026-06-03, then monthly to 2026-10-01
F23.lineage: dates: runs from June, a September showing, the October announcement

F24.quote: Any average describes almost nobody here: a small group embed metadata thoroughly, and 321 of 425 publishers embed none we can find at all.
F24.claim: the distribution: a small group embeds metadata thoroughly; 321 of 425 embed none
F24.lineage: findings: credit and the scored fields (October 2026)

F25.locus: overview, 'How the scores are distributed', note

F25.claim: the stated limit: publishers reached without a photograph are listed as no_images, not scored zero, as the crawler's blind spot
F25.lineage: stated limits: access blocked, the crawler's blind spots

F26.quote: Metawatch · A project of the International Press Telecommunications Council . Data licensed CC BY 4.0 . … Publishers may opt out by emailing office@iptc.org .
F26.claim: a project of the IPTC; data CC BY 4.0; publishers may opt out by email
F26.lineage: open data, cadence and the operator

F27.claim: Paul Melcher's LinkedIn post (14 September 2026, by its card): the IPTC now publishes Metawatch, crawling news publishers monthly (title and snippet only)
F27.lineage: dates: runs from June, a September showing, the October announcement

F28.lineage: the method: the lead photograph of up to 20 articles from each of 508 publishers, scored on the 4 Cs

F29.lineage: findings: credit and the scored fields (October 2026)

F30.quote: DigitalSourceType tracked 15 6,514 0.2% … AIPromptInformation tracked 0 6,514 0% … AISystemUsed tracked 0 6,514 0%
F30.claim: the AI-related fields: DigitalSourceType on 0.2% (15 images); AIPromptInformation and AISystemUsed on none
F30.lineage: AI: crawler blocking, the data-mining field, Content Credentials, the AI fields

F31.quote: Even the best-populated field — Creator at 7.9% — appears on fewer than one in ten images we fetched. The fields most relevant to licensing ( WebStatement , LicensorURL ) are below 3%. The dataset as a whole tells a consistent story: publishers and CDNs are discarding metadata that the photographers and agencies almost certainly embedded upstream.
F31.claim: the reading of the dataset: even Creator is on fewer than one in ten images; licensing fields below 3%; publishers and CDNs discard metadata embedded upstream
F31.lineage: where the stripping happens: the publishing pipeline

F32.quote: Sep 8 2026 … Last Thursday, the photo metadata industry came together for the 2026 IPTC Photo Metadata Conference.

F34.quote: Lastly, Brendan Quinn appeared again to introduce Metawatch , IPTC’s new public service that monitors real-world usage of metadata in images across the global news industry, tracking IPTC/XMP, C2PA, AI opt-outs and more.
F34.claim: Brendan Quinn introduced Metawatch at the conference: the IPTC's new public service monitoring real-world usage of metadata in images across the news industry (IPTC/XMP, C2PA, AI opt-outs)
